extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (especially genre authors) pitching to agents/editors/booksellers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on creating and using 'comp titles' (comparative titles) to describe a book by referencing other works, for clarifying a manuscript, targeting an audience, and pitching to industry professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of comp titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Comp titles (comparative titles) are titles that a book reminds you of — things you use to describe your project in terms of other works.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as a proxy to answer 'Who is this book for?' and to communicate quickly what a book will feel like to someone familiar with other titles. Examples in the episode: 'Home Alone in Space', 'Jane Austen with magic'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Venn-diagram overlap, not the sum
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of comp titles as the narrow overlap between book A and book B (the intersection), not the combination of everything from both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The overlap defines the core elements of your book; avoid implying you get all elements of both comps. This helps define genre and audience more precisely (e.g., 'Star Wars meets Jurassic Park' should indicate which elements from each are present).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comp titles as an early clarifying exercise
rubrics_metrics.description: Come up with comp titles early in the writing process to help refine what you are working on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using comp titles early can reveal which element of the Venn diagram your story occupies; it helps focus core elements and can influence the development of the manuscript and later marketing copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Define genre and category with comp titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Comp titles do a lot of the work to define genre and what category your book fits into before detailed explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They can signal elemental genres (e.g., thriller, horror, space opera) and set expectations for readers and industry professionals about tone and structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify target audience / market positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Comp titles function as a proxy for audience: they tell publishing professionals who the book is for and can affect how many copies it’s likely to sell.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose comps that point to a specific audience niche rather than a franchise with mass appeal; poor choice can show a market isn’t ready or misposition the book (example: Dan’s YA cyberpunk pitched as 'Veronica Mars meets Bladerunner' predated market readiness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider set dressing vs structure
rubrics_metrics.description: When picking comp titles, think separately about 'set dressing' (surface elements like dinosaurs, castles, spaceships) and 'structure' (plot types, thriller vs romance vs horror).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for comp titles whose set dressing and structure align with what you want the reader to expect; mismatch can send a false message (anti-pattern example: 'Jurassic Park' set dressing with a gentle structure unless another comp corrects it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be explicit about which elements you mean
rubrics_metrics.description: You don't have to mean whole books — state which aspects you're referencing (voice, worldbuilding, plot, structure, character type).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrase comp titles like 'the voice of A and the worldbuilding of B' or 'plot of X meets set dressing of Y' to avoid ambiguity. Example: 'Arthur C. Clarke big idea story as told by Octavia Butler.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a third element for a twist
rubrics_metrics.description: You can add a third element or persona (a 'wrench') to the comp to give a twist or highlight a distinctive aspect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The Stand meets Battlestar Galactica, starring Hermione Granger' — the third element (Hermione Granger) indicates a particular character type and modifies expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overused/broad franchise comps
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't use massively broad or overused comps like 'Harry Potter', 'Star Wars', or 'Game of Thrones' as your core comp title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are anti-patterns because they imply the audience is 'every human' and give little useful information; if you must reference a huge franchise, cherry-pick an element (e.g., 'starring Hermione Granger') to be specific.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comp titles work best with industry insiders
rubrics_metrics.description: Comp-title shorthand communicates most effectively to agents, editors, publishers, and booksellers who 'speak that language.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When talking to general readers, expand the comp into a longer sentence so the non-insider audience understands which elements you mean (example: 'Hidden Figures meets Deep Impact' followed by a brief explanation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use comp titles as the base for longer explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the comp title as a starting point from which longer pitch copy descends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After giving a comp, clarify which parts to focus on and expand into a quick elevator pitch that plants a hook or question for the reader ('Hidden Figures meets Deep Impact — so how bad does it get?').

rubrics_metrics.name: Make comp titles invite a question/hook
rubrics_metrics.description: A good comp title plus a short follow-up should plant a hook that invites curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for pitches that leave the listener wanting to know more; the comp should suggest stakes or conflict that prompts a question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure accuracy and avoid misleading signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Be careful that your chosen comps don't mislead about tone, structure, or content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If one comp implies a thriller structure and another implies gentle tone, you risk false expectations; align chosen comps or clarify which elements you're borrowing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comp titles reveal market readiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Comp titles can show whether a book fits existing market trends or whether it might be ahead of its time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comps to assess saleability and marketing strategy; a good comp can help an editor justify resources, while a poor-market-fit comp can explain tepid sales historically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cherry-pick referents rather than invoke whole franchises
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than invoking an entire franchise, pick a specific, describable element (e.g., a type of character or a specific voice) as shorthand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saying 'starring Hermione Granger' conveys a character-type quickly without the unhelpful breadth of 'Harry Potter.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept different comp-title forms (one book + extra element)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comp titles can be one book plus an extra element, not only 'A meets B' two-book constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both approaches are valid — choose whichever conveys the intended audience and core elements succinctly (examples given: one-book-plus-element pitches used successfully by the hosts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice exercise / procedural homework
rubrics_metrics.description: Exercise: Come up with six comp titles — three for existing works-in-progress and three for projects you might want to write.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The exercise is intended to clarify current projects and to serve as brainstorming seeds for new ones; the hosts recommend doing this as concrete practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of conservatism in publishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing can be conservative; lack of a prior successful example makes it harder for something very new to get traction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use comps to place your book within recognizable precedent to increase acceptability, but recognize there are breakout exceptions.
